description: Mahur, among the Sahyadri hills of Nanded district and also called Mahurgad, is the seat of Goddess Renuka, mother of Parashurama in Hindu tradition. The temple is counted among the Shakta pithas of Maharashtra, and tradition holds that it marks the spot where her head fell; the shrine is described as housing a self-manifested image of which only the head is visible. According to the Nanded district website, a Yadava king of Devgiri built it roughly 800 to 900 years ago. The town is also revered as the birthplace of Dattatreya, with a shrine on Datta Shikhar, the highest of its three hills. Pilgrims climb stone steps to the hilltop shrines, and a large fair is held each year at Dasara.

description: Lenyadri, about 5 km north of Junnar in Pune district, is home to the Girijatmaj shrine, one of the eight Ashtavinayak Ganesha temples of Maharashtra. Ganesha is worshipped here as Girijatmaj, the son of Girija (Parvati), in the form of a naturally formed stone figure covered in sindoor. The shrine occupies Cave 7, originally a Buddhist monastic hall, within a group of about thirty rock-cut Buddhist caves dated to roughly the 1st to 3rd centuries AD. According to tradition, Parvati performed twelve years of austerity here and Ganesha was born on Ganesh Chaturthi. Devotees climb several hundred stone steps to reach the cave, and the caves are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

description: Dehu, on the Indrayani river in Pune district, is the home village of Sant Tukaram (1608-1650), the Marathi Warkari poet-saint remembered for abhang verses addressed to Vitthal. According to Wikipedia, his son Narayanbaba built the original temple on the riverbank in 1723. The complex includes the Shila Mandir, a stone shrine with a statue of the saint, linked to the rock on which, according to tradition, he sat for thirteen days when his abhangs were challenged; the Prime Minister inaugurated it in June 2022. The nearby Gatha Mandir has about 4,000 of his abhangs carved on its walls, and the Tukaram Palkhi procession to Pandharpur sets out from Dehu in the month of Ashadh, making it a major Warkari pilgrimage place.

description: Kailasa Temple, excavated as Cave 16 at Ellora, is a Shiva temple cut out of a basalt hillside in Maharashtra and named after Mount Kailash, the god's legendary Himalayan home. According to Britannica and the Archaeological Survey of India, work began under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I in the 8th century. Unlike most caves, it was carved downward from the top of the rock, leaving a freestanding temple with a gateway, a Nandi shrine, a main sanctum rising about 23 metres, four subsidiary shrines and cloisters around a courtyard. Plinth panels show elephants, lions and scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Ellora Caves. It is a protected monument.

description: The Elephanta Caves are a group of seven rock-cut cave excavations on Elephanta Island, also called Gharapuri, in Mumbai harbour. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Cave 1, the largest, is devoted to Shiva. Its entrance is dominated by a sculpture about 7 metres high, Sadashiva, showing three aspects of the god, and panels include Ardhanarishvara, Nataraja, Gangadhara and Shiva and Parvati playing chausar. Cave 1 measures 39 metres from front to back and its plan resembles Dumar Lena at Ellora. The ASI dates the caves to roughly the 6th-7th centuries CE, while UNESCO gives the mid-5th to 6th centuries. The island is named after a colossal elephant statue now kept in Jijamata Garden, Mumbai.

description: Rukmini Devi Temple in Dwarka, Gujarat, is dedicated to Rukmini, the chief consort of Krishna, who is regarded as an incarnation of Lakshmi. Incredible India places it about 2 km from the Dwarkadhish Temple. Tradition holds that the shrine goes back to the 5th century BC, but Gujarat Tourism says the present temple dates from the 12th century and may have been rebuilt, while Wikipedia says the present structure is believed to be 19th century. The shikhara is in Nagara style, with carved gods and goddesses on the walls and panels of human figures and elephants at the base. According to legend, the sage Durvasa cursed Rukmini to live apart from Krishna after she drank water before offering him any, which explains the separate temples.

description: The Amba Mata temple stands on the first peak of Girnar, the hill above Junagadh that carries both Hindu and Jain shrines. Gujarat Tourism says newly married couples come here to pray for a happy marriage. Wikipedia's Girnar article identifies the shrine as the Ambika temple, dedicated to Ambika, a Jain yakshini who attends the 22nd Tirthankara, Neminatha, and dates the present building to about the 15th century. According to that article, an inscription of 1192 CE records a pilgrimage by the minister Vastupala, and a 1468 CE eulogy credits the merchant Samal Sah with renovating it. A ropeway, inaugurated in October 2020, rises to the temple; the full walking route to the summit is about 10,000 stone steps.

description: The Hutheesing Jain Temple, also called Hathisingh Derasar, is a white marble Shvetambara Jain temple outside Delhi Darwaza in Shahibaug, Ahmedabad. Its main sanctuary is dedicated to Dharmanatha, the 15th Tirthankara. It opened in 1848. Hathisinh Kesarisinh, an Ahmedabad businessman, began it partly to give work to artisans in a famine; he died during construction and his wife, Harkunvar, completed it. Premchand Salat is named as the master craftsman. A pillared cloister around the courtyard holds 52 subsidiary shrines with marble images, and a Manastambha tower with a Mahavira statue stands in front. The temple retains its original rainwater harvesting system and is the largest of Ahmedabad's Jain temples.

description: Kesariyaji, also called Rishabhdev or Kesariyanath, is a temple at Rishabhdeo (Dhulev) in Udaipur district. Its black stone image of Rishabhanatha, the first Jain Tirthankara, is about 3.5 feet tall and seated in padmasana. The name Kesariya comes from the large quantity of saffron offered to the deity. Jains of both Shvetambara and Digambara traditions visit, and local Bhil and Meena communities also revere the image, with Bhils calling it Kalaji or Kalababa. According to tradition, a Bhil man named Dhula found the idol. The complex has 52 shrines,. Wikipedia says the origins are unclear, with belief in an 8th-century date.

description: Galtaji, also called Galwar Bagh and widely nicknamed the Monkey Temple, is a Hindu pilgrimage complex in a narrow cleft of the Aravalli hills about 10 km east of Jaipur. It is linked with the sage Galav, who by tradition performed penance here and was rewarded with abundant water. A spring feeds a chain of sacred kunds (tanks) where pilgrims bathe, and the Galta Kund is regarded as the holiest. The pink sandstone buildings, with domed pavilions, carved pillars and painted walls, resemble a haveli more than an ordinary temple. The complex includes a Ramgopalji shrine to Vishnu and a hilltop Sun temple, and it has long been a centre for Ramanandi Vaishnava ascetics. Large crowds bathe at Makar Sankranti, and rhesus macaques live throughout the site.

description: Shila Devi is a form of the goddess Durga, worshipped in a Shakta temple at Amer Fort near Jaipur and counted among the region's prominent Shakti shrines. The image is carved from stone, which gives the deity her name. According to tradition, Maharaja Man Singh I was blessed by the goddess in a dream and brought a stone slab from eastern Bengal; the image took its present form after being cleaned at Amer. Sources disagree on the founding date, giving 1580 and 1604. The Devasthan Department describes carved pillars and panels, a sanctum with four verandahs, and regular recitation of the Durga Saptashati. Special worship is held during Navaratri in Ashwin and Chaitra, when the temple draws large numbers of devotees.

description: Jeen Mata is a form of Shakti worshipped in a hill temple in the Aravalli range, in Sikar district. The Devasthan Department describes the image as Mahishasura Mardini Durga with eight arms and gives the construction date as unknown, citing a stone inscription as evidence of age. Local belief links the site to a woman named Jeen who practised austerity here and to the Pandavas' exile; a popular tradition, noted on Wikipedia, places the temple in the eighth century. The sanctum is marble with silver shutters, and a 24-pillared hall and tall shikhar follow Pratihara and Chauhan styles. A Bhramari Devi shrine stands behind. Devotees visit on the bright eighth of each month, bring infants for a first hair-cutting rite, and gather in large numbers at Chaitra and Ashwin Navaratri.
